**Internal Engineering Memo**

**To:** Platform and Applied AI Teams  
**From:** Engineering Strategy  
**Subject:** Local AI Capacity: Buy More Hardware or Use What We Have Better  
**Date:** 21 June 2026

We need to make a near-term decision about local AI capacity. The question in front of us is deceptively simple: should we purchase additional GPUs and supporting infrastructure, or should we invest engineering effort in improving utilisation of the machines we already own? The answer matters not only because hardware is expensive, but because the choice will shape how we build, schedule, measure, and operate our AI systems over the next several quarters. My recommendation is that we should not buy more hardware yet. We should first commit to a focused utilisation programme, with a defined review point and explicit triggers for procurement if the evidence changes.

The current pressure is real. Teams are seeing longer queues for fine-tuning jobs, intermittent contention for inference capacity, and occasional delays when evaluation runs collide with product demos or customer-facing experiments. These symptoms naturally lead to the conclusion that we are capacity-constrained. But queueing and frustration are not the same as sustained saturation. Our preliminary telemetry suggests that average GPU utilisation is materially below what we would expect from a well-scheduled fleet, with sharp peaks, long idle gaps, and a meaningful amount of capacity consumed by jobs that are poorly sized, duplicated, or left running longer than necessary. Before we convert capital expenditure into more idle cycles, we should determine whether the bottleneck is physical compute or the software and operational layer around it.

Cost is the most visible factor, but it is not only the purchase price. Additional accelerators imply servers, networking, power, cooling, rack space, spares, firmware compatibility work, driver validation, monitoring, and the ongoing tax of heterogeneous capacity. Even when the sticker price is acceptable, the total cost of ownership includes the engineering time required to integrate new nodes into the cluster and keep them reliable. There is also an opportunity cost: money and attention spent on procurement cannot simultaneously fund better batching, caching, model distillation, quantisation, scheduler improvements, observability, or product work that reduces demand. If we can recover even a modest fraction of existing capacity through software and process changes, that capacity is effectively cheaper than new hardware and arrives without a long lead time.

Latency deserves separate treatment because it is often where the buy-more argument is strongest. For interactive inference, especially customer-facing features, tail latency is a product requirement rather than an internal convenience. More hardware can reduce queueing delay and provide headroom for traffic spikes. However, utilisation work can also improve latency if the real problem is noisy co-tenancy, poor admission control, inefficient batching, cold model loads, or jobs with no priority separation. We should be careful not to use average utilisation as a proxy for user experience. A fleet can look underused overall while still failing at p95 or p99 during bursts. The right first step is to distinguish interactive service-level objectives from batch experimentation capacity, then measure whether our current scheduling and isolation mechanisms are allowing one class of workload to harm another. If they are, reserved pools, preemption policies, model residency, and request routing may deliver more predictable latency than simply adding nodes.

Reliability cuts both ways. A larger fleet can improve redundancy and reduce the blast radius of a failed node, but it also increases the number of components that can fail and the complexity of failover. New hardware introduces a period of instability: driver mismatches, thermal issues, memory errors, uneven performance, and subtle differences between device generations. Our existing environment is understood, monitored, and mostly debugged. Improving utilisation through better orchestration can also improve reliability if it includes health checks, retry semantics, checkpointing, graceful degradation, and clearer workload priorities. On the other hand, running the current fleet closer to its limits will reduce slack. That is acceptable only if we define what slack is for: absorbing node failure, handling traffic spikes, or protecting critical jobs. Higher utilisation should not mean eliminating all margin; it should mean making margin intentional rather than accidental.

Reversibility strongly favours the utilisation-first path. Engineering work on scheduling, observability, batching, model optimisation, and workload classification is largely reversible and often reusable even if we later buy hardware. A better scheduler remains valuable on a larger cluster. Cleaner job metadata remains valuable if we move some workloads to a cloud provider. Procurement is much less reversible. Hardware has lead times, depreciation, resale friction, and a tendency to anchor future architecture decisions. Once bought, there is organisational pressure to use it, even if demand patterns shift toward smaller models, external APIs, or managed inference. In an environment where model architectures, quantisation support, and vendor roadmaps are changing quickly, preserving optionality has real value.

That said, uncertainty is substantial. Our current measurements are incomplete, and utilisation metrics can be misleading: GPU busy time does not capture memory pressure, interconnect contention, data-loading stalls, or the strategic value of keeping capacity free for urgent work. Demand may also grow faster than expected if a new product feature succeeds, if evaluation requirements expand, or if we bring more training in-house for privacy reasons. Supply constraints and pricing changes could make delayed procurement more expensive. There is also a human cost to asking teams to wait: repeated contention erodes trust and encourages local workarounds, shadow infrastructure, and overly conservative experiment design. We should take that seriously rather than treating utilisation as a purely technical optimisation.

For those reasons, I recommend a time-boxed utilisation programme before any expansion purchase. Over the next six to eight weeks, we should instrument the fleet well enough to separate interactive, batch, training, evaluation, and development workloads; introduce priority-aware scheduling and reserved capacity for latency-sensitive services; eliminate obvious waste through job timeouts, checkpointing, deduplication, and right-sizing; and publish a small set of shared metrics covering sustained utilisation, queue time, tail latency, failure recovery, and engineer-visible delay. In parallel, we should prepare a procurement option—configuration, budget, lead time, and integration plan—so that buying remains fast if needed. The decision to buy should be triggered by evidence such as sustained high utilisation after optimisation, repeated breach of service-level objectives despite isolation, or a committed product roadmap whose demand cannot be met by known efficiency gains.

This is not an argument against owning more capacity. It is an argument against treating hardware as the first response to a system whose bottlenecks we have not yet fully characterised. If we buy now, we risk paying to preserve inefficiency and reducing our flexibility at precisely the moment when flexibility is most valuable. If we improve utilisation first, we either solve the problem cheaply and quickly, or we generate the evidence needed to buy with confidence. In both cases, we end up with a platform that is easier to operate, easier to reason about, and better aligned with the actual shape of demand.

**Internal Engineering Memo**

**To:** Platform and Applied AI Teams  
**From:** Engineering Strategy  
**Subject:** Local AI Capacity: Buy More Hardware or Use What We Have Better  
**Date:** 2026-07-14  

We need to make a near-term decision about local AI capacity. The question in front of us is deceptively simple: should we purchase additional GPUs and supporting infrastructure, or should we invest engineering effort in improving utilisation of the machines we already own? My recommendation is that we should not buy more hardware yet. We should first commit to a focused utilisation programme, with a defined review point, because our current constraints appear to be at least as much scheduling, observability, and workload-shape problems as they are raw compute problems. That said, this is not a claim that hardware is unnecessary; it is a claim that buying now would likely lock in cost and complexity before we have extracted the cheaper, more reversible gains available in our existing fleet.

The cost case for delaying purchase is strong, but it is not merely about avoiding capital expense. Additional accelerators bring a stack of committed costs: servers, networking, power, cooling, rack space, spare parts, firmware compatibility work, driver maintenance, and the operational burden of keeping another pool of devices healthy. Even when the sticker price of the GPUs dominates the conversation, the durable cost is the whole system around them. If our current fleet is idle for meaningful portions of the day, or if jobs are queued because memory is fragmented rather than because FLOPs are exhausted, then new hardware would mostly be an expensive way to replicate the same inefficiencies at larger scale. We would also be spending against a depreciating asset class, where waiting can itself have value: prices shift, newer parts arrive, and our workload mix becomes clearer.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side. Some teams are already seeing unpredictable turnaround for fine-tuning runs, evaluation sweeps, and internal inference services. When a researcher waits hours for a job that should take minutes, the cost is not just compute inefficiency; it is lost iteration velocity. Worse, variable latency changes behaviour. People batch work, avoid experiments, keep long-lived processes alive “just in case,” and design around queue uncertainty. Those adaptations can further reduce utilisation and make the system feel slower than it is. If we had dedicated capacity for interactive workloads, or enough headroom to absorb bursts without admission control, we could improve both perceived and actual responsiveness.

But latency is not identical to capacity. A system can have low average utilisation and still produce terrible tail latency if scheduling is coarse, priorities are absent, or large jobs monopolise devices. Our preliminary observations suggest this is happening: a few long-running jobs create head-of-line blocking, while smaller jobs wait despite available memory on partially occupied cards. We also lack a shared, trusted view of who is consuming what, for how long, and with what deadline. In that environment, buying hardware treats the symptom. It may reduce queue pressure temporarily, but it does not give us control over the mechanisms that create the queue.

Reliability also cuts both ways. More machines can improve resilience by adding redundancy and reducing the blast radius of a failed node. A larger fleet can let us drain hosts for maintenance without stopping critical services. Yet more hardware also means more failure domains, more version skew, more networking complexity, and more subtle differences between “identical” nodes. If our current reliability problems stem from job checkpointing, preemption handling, container images, or poor recovery after device errors, additional capacity will not solve them. It may even mask them until the fleet is larger and the operational debt is harder to unwind. Improving utilisation work should therefore include reliability primitives: checkpointing, graceful preemption, retry semantics, health checks, and workload placement that accounts for node condition. These are useful whether or not we later expand.

The opportunity cost is perhaps the most important consideration. Engineering attention is finite. A utilisation programme means several weeks of work on scheduling, telemetry, batching, model placement, mixed-precision defaults, caching, and possibly quota policy. That is time not spent on product features, model quality, or customer-facing reliability. However, a hardware purchase also consumes attention: procurement, vendor coordination, installation, burn-in, cluster integration, capacity planning, and ongoing maintenance. The difference is that utilisation work produces knowledge and software assets that remain useful under almost any future hardware decision. It improves our ability to specify what to buy, to forecast when we need it, and to operate it well. Buying first gives us capacity, but it does not necessarily give us understanding.

Reversibility favours the same path. Software and process improvements can usually be iterated, rolled back, or redirected. A scheduler policy can be changed; a telemetry dashboard can be expanded; a quota can be relaxed. Hardware purchases are much less reversible. They commit us to a particular vendor, power envelope, interconnect assumptions, and utilisation target. Even if the equipment can be resold, the integration effort and organisational momentum are sunk. In a small team, irreversible decisions deserve a higher burden of proof, especially when the underlying demand signal is noisy.

I recommend a six-week utilisation-first phase. During that period we should instrument the fleet well enough to distinguish compute saturation from memory fragmentation, queueing policy, data-loading stalls, and avoidable idle time. We should introduce basic priority classes for interactive, scheduled, and best-effort work; improve batching and co-location where safe; enforce checkpointing for long jobs; and set explicit service expectations for internal inference. At the end, we should review tail latency, job completion time, effective GPU-hours delivered, failure recovery, and engineer experience. If, after those changes, sustained demand still exceeds a sensible utilisation ceiling—say, if we cannot preserve acceptable latency without running the fleet at unhealthy occupancy—then we should buy, and we will be able to buy with much better evidence.

The uncertainty is real. Our workload may grow faster than expected, especially if a new model evaluation pipeline or customer-adjacent feature becomes urgent. Hardware lead times may lengthen. Some latency requirements may be non-negotiable. It is also possible that utilisation work reveals not inefficiency but genuine saturation, in which case the delay will have cost us several weeks of constrained throughput. We should mitigate this by defining escalation triggers in advance and by keeping a lightweight procurement path warm, without committing funds.

For now, the prudent choice is to treat our existing fleet as a system to be understood and improved, not merely a pool of devices to be enlarged. The decision is not “hardware versus engineering”; it is about sequencing. Better utilisation is cheaper, more informative, and more reversible. If we still need more machines afterward, we will know why, how many, and what kind.

**Internal Engineering Memo**

**To:** Platform and Applied AI Teams  
**From:** Engineering Strategy  
**Subject:** Local AI Capacity: Buy More Hardware or Use What We Have Better  
**Date:** 2026-07-14  

We need to make a near-term decision about local AI capacity. The question in front of us is deceptively simple: should we purchase additional GPUs and supporting infrastructure, or should we invest engineering effort in improving utilisation of the machines we already own? My recommendation is that we should not buy more hardware yet. We should commit a focused four-to-six-week effort to measurement, scheduling, batching, model routing, and workload shaping, with a predefined threshold that would justify a purchase if utilisation improvements do not close the gap. This is not a blanket “do more with less” position. It is a sequencing decision based on cost, latency, reliability, opportunity cost, and the reversibility of the two paths.

The direct cost of new hardware is the easiest part to see and, in some ways, the least important. A incremental purchase is not just the price of accelerators. It includes host machines, networking, power, cooling, rack space, spare capacity, maintenance, firmware and driver validation, monitoring integration, and the staff time required to make the new nodes production-ready. Even if the capital expense is approved quickly, the useful capacity arrives only after procurement, delivery, installation, burn-in, and rollout. That delay matters because our current pain is not abstract future demand; it is present queueing, unpredictable turnaround, and occasional contention between interactive workloads and long-running jobs. Buying hardware solves a capacity problem eventually, but it does not necessarily solve the scheduling and prioritisation problems that are producing much of the visible latency today.

Latency deserves particular attention because “more hardware” and “lower latency” are not synonymous. If our queues are caused by poor admission control, lack of preemption, inefficient batching, or jobs holding devices while waiting on CPU preprocessing or remote data, then adding nodes may simply allow more inefficient work to pile up. We have already seen cases where a model server reserves a GPU for a request that spends a meaningful fraction of its wall-clock time waiting on tokenisation, feature retrieval, or network I/O. In those cases, the accelerator is nominally busy but not doing useful accelerator work. A utilisation programme would force us to distinguish between device occupancy, useful compute, memory pressure, and end-to-end service time. That distinction is likely to produce better latency outcomes than raw expansion, especially for interactive traffic where tail latency is shaped by queue discipline and isolation as much as by average throughput.

Reliability also cuts both ways. More hardware increases theoretical redundancy, but it also increases the operational surface area: more drivers, more interconnects, more thermal variance, more failure domains, and more configuration drift. If we add capacity without first improving our ability to drain nodes, checkpoint jobs, retry safely, and route around degraded devices, we may create a larger but still brittle pool. Conversely, better utilisation can improve reliability if it includes health-aware scheduling, workload quotas, graceful degradation, and clearer service tiers. There is a risk, however, that pushing utilisation too high leaves no headroom for failures or bursts. A system running at 95% sustained occupancy can look efficient right up until one node fails and the entire queue collapses. Our target should therefore be effective utilisation with explicit reserve capacity, not maximum occupancy.

The opportunity cost is probably the strongest argument for delaying purchase. Every week spent evaluating vendors, validating hardware, and expanding the cluster is a week not spent improving inference paths, caching, quantisation, request coalescing, asynchronous pipelines, or model selection. Some of those improvements reduce not only local congestion but also cloud fallback spend and developer wait time. They are portable: if we later buy hardware, the same scheduling and efficiency work makes the new hardware more valuable. If we later move more workloads to hosted inference, the work still helps by reducing request volume and improving fallback behaviour. Hardware purchases, by contrast, are comparatively specific. They assume that our current workload mix, model sizes, and local-deployment requirements will remain stable long enough to amortise the investment. That may be true, but it is not yet demonstrated.

Reversibility favours the utilisation-first path as well. Engineering work can be stopped, redirected, or incrementally adopted. A scheduler change can be rolled back. A batching policy can be tuned. A routing rule can be scoped to one service. A hardware purchase is much harder to unwind, especially once it has been integrated into capacity plans and team expectations. Even when equipment has resale value, the organisational commitment is sticky: once we own more capacity, teams will design around it, and we will be less likely to question inefficient workloads. Starting with utilisation preserves optionality. It gives us better data about whether the constraint is truly compute, or whether it is memory bandwidth, data locality, queue policy, model choice, or simply uncoordinated demand.

That said, there is real uncertainty here. Our current telemetry is not good enough to prove that utilisation work will be sufficient. We do not yet have a clean breakdown of queue time by workload class, a reliable measure of useful GPU compute versus idle reservation, or a forecast that separates steady-state demand from launch spikes. It is possible that demand is growing faster than any reasonable software optimisation can offset. It is also possible that some upcoming models have memory footprints that make current nodes structurally unsuitable, regardless of scheduling efficiency. We should acknowledge this openly rather than treating the utilisation effort as a way to avoid a decision. The next few weeks should produce evidence: baseline utilisation, p50/p95/p99 latency by service tier, failure and retry rates, job preemption behaviour, cloud fallback cost, and a demand forecast tied to named workloads rather than general optimism.

My recommendation is to pause new hardware procurement for one measurement-and-improvement cycle, with a small team chartered to improve utilisation and observability. We should set a decision point in advance. If, after that cycle, interactive tail latency remains above target during normal load, sustained useful utilisation remains high with appropriate failure headroom, and forecast demand still exceeds the improved capacity, then we should buy hardware with a much better specification and a clearer business case. If utilisation work resolves the bottlenecks, we will have avoided an expensive, irreversible expansion and built capabilities that compound over time. In either case, we will be making the purchase decision with facts rather than with the discomfort of a queue. The prudent choice is not “never buy”; it is “earn the right to buy by first understanding and improving the system we already have.”
